To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
AtDRP1As purified as a maltose binding protein fusion polymerize and interact with liposomes, but do not have the capacity to tubulate them.
AtDRP1 forms homopolymeric polymers that interact with protein-free, negatively charged liposomes, suggesting that lipids are involved in its in vivo function.
the GTPase active form of the Arabidopsiss endocytic dynamin-related protein, AtDRP-1A, purified from E. coli as a maltose binding protein fusion, forms polymers that bind to liposomes in vitro.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of AtDRP1 in the endocytosis of the Arabidospis plasma membrane and the formation of new cell walls.
the molecular mechanisms of endocytic and secretory trafficking.
the role of dynamin-like proteins in the formation of the cell plate in plants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the AtDRP1 protein does not tubulate liposomes and therefore is not a true dynamin.
AtDRP1a polymers bind lipids but not proteins, and that they have no tubulation ability.
AtDRP1a polymers do not have the capacity to tubulate liposomal membranes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
AtDRP1As form polymers in vitro and that these polymers can bind protein-free liposomes, however the AtDRP1 polymers do not have the same ability as dynamin to tubulate lipids in vitro.
we report the purification and biochemical characterization of the first dynamin-related protein in plants.
AtDRP1 is a GTPase that can form polymers and bind liposomes but that these properties are not sufficient for its in vivo function.
The main takeaway from our work is that
AtDRP1 polymers are able to bind to lipid membranes, but that the mechanism of membrane binding and the role of membrane binding in AtDRP function remains to be determined.
AtDRP1 is capable of binding lipids, and therefore may play a direct role in membrane remodeling.
